payload.previous_feedback: Previous vetter reason: The proof is a correct standard argument from the definition of floor: if m = floor(x), then m <= x and m+1 cannot be <= x, otherwise m would not be greatest. Therefore x < m+1 = floor(x)+1. The proof matches the lemma exactly and uses only allowed notions.
payload.previous_proof_nl: Let x be any real number and set m = floor(x). By the definition of the floor function, m is an integer, m <= x, and m is the greatest integer with this property. Suppose, for contradiction, that x >= m + 1. Then m + 1 is also an integer, and m + 1 <= x. This contradicts the maximality of m as the greatest integer less than or equal to x. Hence x < m + 1 = floor(x) + 1. Since x was arbitrary, the statement holds for every real number x.

payload.statement_nl: For every real number x, x < floor(x) + 1.

result_payload.addressed_previous_feedback: The previous feedback indicated the proof was already correct and standard. I kept the same proof skeleton and made the contradiction step explicit: assuming x >= floor(x)+1 produces an integer larger than floor(x) that is still <= x, contradicting the defining maximality of floor(x).
result_payload.proof_nl: Let x be any real number, and set m = floor(x). By the definition of the floor function, m is an integer and m <= x, and moreover m is the greatest integer with this property. Suppose for contradiction that x >= m + 1. Then m + 1 is also an integer, and m + 1 <= x. This contradicts the maximality of m, since m + 1 > m is an integer still not exceeding x. Therefore x < m + 1. Since m = floor(x), we obtain x < floor(x) + 1. Because x was arbitrary, the statement holds for every real number x.
result_payload.proof_summary: Use the defining maximality property of floor(x): if m = floor(x), then m is the greatest integer <= x. If x were at least m+1, then m+1 would be an integer <= x, contradicting maximality. Hence x < floor(x)+1 for all real x.
